title: What is Git?
description: Git is a free and open-source distributed version control system (VCS) designed to handle everything from small to very large projects with speed and efficiency.
points: Created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 to manage Linux kernel development.
Tracks changes across files over time, allowing you to recall specific versions later.
Operates completely offline on your local machine without needing an internet connection.
Every developer's clone is a full repository with complete history and revision-tracking capabilities.
example:
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Save milestone snapshot"

title: What is GitHub?
description: GitHub is a cloud-based hosting service and collaboration platform for Git repositories. It provides a web interface, social coding, and automation tools.
points: Hosts your remote Git repositories securely in the cloud.
Facilitates team collaboration through Pull Requests, code reviews, and issue tracking.
Offers free static website hosting via GitHub Pages.
Provides CI/CD workflow automation through GitHub Actions.
Serves as the global hub for open-source software with over 100M+ developers.

title: Git vs GitHub: Key Differences
description: Beginners frequently confuse Git and GitHub. Git is the underlying version control tool running locally, while GitHub is a cloud hosting service.

comparison.github: Runs on remote servers in the cloud

comparison.git: Tracks file changes and commit history
comparison.github: Shares repositories and enables team collaboration

title: Version Control System (VCS)
description: A system that records changes to a file or set of files over time so you can recall specific versions, compare differences, and collaborate without stepping on teammates' toes.
points: Local VCS: Simple database that kept all changes to files under revision control.
Centralized VCS (e.g. SVN): Single server containing all versioned files. Risk: single point of failure.
Distributed VCS (e.g. Git): Every checkout is a full mirror of the entire repository history. If a server dies, any client repo can restore it.
example:
# View full project timeline
git log --oneline --graph

title: Repository (Repo)
description: A Git repository is essentially a directory containing all your project files alongside a hidden '.git' directory that houses the entire version database and history.
points: Local Repository: Stored on your own machine's filesystem.
Remote Repository: Hosted on GitHub, GitLab, or an internal server.
The '.git' folder contains all commits, branches, tags, and configuration data.
example:
# Initialize in current folder
git init

# Or clone from remote
git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git

title: Commit (Snapshot)
description: A commit records changes to the repository. Unlike other VCS tools that store file differences, Git thinks of its data more like a set of snapshots of a miniature filesystem.
points: Every commit has a unique 40-character SHA-1/SHA-256 hash (e.g. 7f8a3b2...).
Records who made the change (Author & Committer) and exact timestamp.
Requires a clear message describing why and what changed.
Commits are immutable: you never lose history unless explicitly forced.
example: git commit -m "feat: Add user authentication middleware"

title: Branch
description: A branch in Git is simply a lightweight, movable pointer to one of your commits. The default branch name in modern Git repositories is 'main'.
points: Branching is virtually instantaneous and consumes minimal disk space.
Enables developers to work on new features, experiment, or fix bugs without destabilizing production code.
Allows multiple team members to work on separate tasks simultaneously.
example:
# Create and switch
git switch -c feature-dashboard

# Return to main
git switch main

title: Merge
description: Merging combines the histories and file changes of two independent branches into a single unified branch.
points: Fast-Forward Merge: Occurs when no divergent commits exist; Git simply moves the branch pointer forward.
3-Way Merge: Occurs when both branches have new commits. Git uses a common ancestor commit to create a new 'merge commit'.
If changes overlap on the same lines, Git flags a Merge Conflict for the developer to resolve.
example:
git switch main
git merge feature-dashboard

title: Clone
description: Cloning copies an entire remote repository onto your local computer, including every version of every file, commit history, and branches.
points: Automatically configures a remote pointer named 'origin' pointing back to the cloned URL.
Checks out the default branch (usually 'main') into your working directory.
You only need to clone a repository once; subsequent updates are received using 'git pull'.

title: Fork
description: A fork is a server-side copy of someone else's GitHub repository managed under your own GitHub account.
points: Allows you to freely experiment and make changes without affecting the original project.
Standard starting point for open-source contributions.
You can push to your fork and submit your improvements back to the original author via a Pull Request.
example:
# After clicking 'Fork' on GitHub:
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/forked-repo.git
git remote add upstream https://github.com/ORIGINAL-OWNER/repo.git

title: Pull Request (PR)
description: A Pull Request is a GitHub mechanism to notify team members that you have completed a feature and want your changes merged into another branch.
points: Provides a dedicated web interface for side-by-side code diffs and inline discussions.
Allows team leads to review code quality and enforce automated tests before merging.
Can be updated anytime by simply pushing new commits to the source branch.
example:
git push origin feature-payments
# Then click 'Compare & pull request' on GitHub

title: Merge Conflict
description: A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically resolve differences in code between two commits, typically when two branches modify the exact same line.
points: Git stops the merge process and marks the affected files with special conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>).
Never fear conflicts: they are an intentional safeguard preventing Git from silently guessing and destroying your code.
Resolved manually by choosing which lines to keep, removing markers, staging, and committing.
example:
<<<<<<< HEAD
const api = 'https://api.v1.local';
=======
const api = 'https://api.v2.production';
>>>>>>> origin/main

title: .gitignore File
description: A plain text file placed in your repository root that tells Git which files, folders, and patterns to intentionally ignore and exclude from version control.
points: Prevents sensitive data like API keys, passwords, and .env files from leaking to GitHub.
Prevents bloating the repository with build artifacts, logs, node_modules/, and OS files (.DS_Store).
Only applies to untracked files; files already tracked by Git must be unstaged with 'git rm --cached'.

title: README.md
description: The digital welcome mat of your repository. GitHub automatically displays the contents of README.md on the repository homepage.
points: Written in Markdown (.md) syntax supporting headings, bolding, lists, code blocks, and images.
Crucial for communicating project purpose, installation instructions, usage examples, and licensing.
A well-crafted README distinguishes high-quality developer projects in college evaluations and job interviews.
example:
# Git & GitHub Assistant
> Your Intelligent Coding Companion

## Installation
`pip install -r requirements.txt`
